sources.news_title: Trump advisers see opportunities for Middle East agenda without Netanyahu
sources.text: Trump advisers see better chance to pursue Mideast agenda if Netanyahu loses October 24, 2026 President Donald Trump points to Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as he speaks with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club, Monday, Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) Trump advisers see better chance to pursue Mideast agenda if Netanyahu loses Tweet Join Group Join WhatsApp Group Email https://worldisraelnews.com/trump-advisers-see-opportunities-for-middle-east-agenda-without-netanyahu/ Email Print Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot currently appears to have a clear path to the 61 seats needed for a government. By Vered Weiss, World Israel News Some of President Donald Trump’s senior advisers believe an Israeli government led by someone other than Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could make it easier to pursue parts of Trump’s Middle East agenda after Tuesday’s election, U.S. officials told Axios. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday after weeks of hesitation, but many of his closest advisers opposed the move because they believed he should stay out of the election, sources familiar with the discussions said. “He’s the devil he knows,” one Trump adviser said of Trump’s view of Netanyahu. Vice President Vance declined to follow Trump’s endorsement this week. “I’m not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I’m not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu. I think the president’s endorsement is ultimately what matters,” Vance told reporters. Sources familiar with their thinking said Vance and other senior officials became disillusioned with Netanyahu during the war with Iran and believe his pre-war assessments to the White House were mistaken. Other disagreements involve Trump’s regional diplomatic priorities. Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been frustrated by Netanyahu’s reluctance to advance Trump’s Gaza peace plan, while envoy Tom Barrack has concerns about Israel’s approach to Damascus and continued military operations in Syria. Read Honoring fallen troops, Trump says Iran war prevented nuclear catastrophe Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his team have a better relationship with Netanyahu but believe Israel could do more to strengthen Lebanon’s government and curb settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. Trump also faces a decision after the Israeli election and U.S. midterms over whether to join Netanyahu in another major military operation against Iran. Netanyahu wants to move forward, while Trump also wants to pursue agreements involving Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Saudi Arabia. Friday’s final pre-election polls from three major Israeli television networks projected Netanyahu’s bloc winning 50 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 52 to 56 for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc. Another 14 to 16 seats were projected for two Arab Israeli parties. Pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, however, projected 60 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc earlier this week. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot currently appears to have a clear path to the 61 seats needed for a government. If neither succeeds, Israel could face another election, leaving Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister. Benjamin NetanyahuDonald TrumpIsraeli election

sources.news_title: Trump advisers say Netanyahu loss could be good for US agenda
sources.text:
Trump advisers still see opportunity for US agenda even if Netanyahu loses: report
See more of our coverage in your search results.
President Trump’s advisers reportedly believe a loss by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s election could actually make it easier to advance the president’s Middle East agenda.
Should Netanyahu — who has served as prime minister for roughly 19 years across three stints — be ousted, his potential successors would have strong incentives to maintain close ties with Washington, US officials told Axios.
The assessment comes as Israelis prepare to vote Oct. 27, with polls showing Netanyahu’s coalition struggling to secure the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.
The potential for progress for Trump’s Middle East agenda in a new political environment comes despite the president’s notable decision to endorse the conservative Likud Party leader last Sunday, while Netanyahu trails in the polls against former Israeli Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Trump called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” in a reference to joint US-Israeli attacks on Iran and Israel’s battle against Hezbollah and other foes.
Several of Trump’s top advisors have grown “dissatisfied” with Netanyahu over key regional priorities over the last six months, Axios reported.
US envoy to Syria Tom Barrack has expressed doubts about Israel’s military operations in Syria, while Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff have been frustrated by what they see as Netanyahu’s reluctance to advance Trump’s peace plan, according to the report.
“He’s the devil he knows,” one Trump advisor said of Netanyahu, who was also in office during the entirety of Trump’s first term.
After the elections, Trump will face a “defining choice” about whether to join Netanyahu in another military operation against Iran. US intelligence is warning Iran is increasing its threats against Americans in the region, US warships including two aircraft carrier strike groups in the region are preparing for a potential escalation.
Trump’s decision to join Netanyahu in a joint attack on Iran in February precipitated a spike in oil prices that has Trump facing stiff headwinds in the midterm elections Nov. 3. But he has said repeatedly the attacks set back Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.
The endorsement also gives Trump the opportunity to try to take credit if Netanyahu wins. Eisenkot, in an interview with The Post, is stressing deep ties between the US and Israel, and spoke positively about Trump’s efforts in the region.
Vice President JD Vance notably did not endorse Netanyahu in an interview Monday with journalist Mark Halperin. “The president has the most influential endorsement in American or international political history,” said Vance. “I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on the midterms.”
Vance traveled to Budapest to boost Hungarian strongman Prime Minister Viktor Orbán shortly before Orban’s defeat.
Trump later commented on his running mate’s posture. “I don’t know that he did or didn’t, that’s up to him,” Trump said Friday. “I would leave that up to him.”

sources.news_title: Trump advisers optimistic about working with Netanyahu's rivals if he loses next election
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump’s advisers are reportedly optimistic about opportunities to work with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s opposition if he loses in the upcoming election, according to US officials cited by Axios.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Tuesday after weeks of hesitation, with Axios noting that the US president has never worked with an Israeli prime minister other than Netanyahu and does not personally know any of the other candidates.
“[Netanyahu] is the devil [Trump] knows,” one Trump adviser told Axios.
The report also said that many of Trump's closest advisers opposed his decision to endorse Netanyahu, believing the president should stay out of the Israeli election.
In contrast, Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu when asked about the election this week. “I'm not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I'm not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu… I think the president's endorsement is ultimately what matters,” Vance told reporters.
The US Ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, raised concerns about the Netanyahu government's approach to Syria and continued Israeli military operations in Syria.
Following Israeli strikes on a base in Syria’s northern Idlib province, Barrack denounced the attack as an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his team have maintained a better relationship with the Prime Minister, but believe Israel could do more to strengthen Lebanon's government. They have also expressed frustration with Netanyahu's failure to do more to curb settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, Axios reported.
Final poll finds opposition increasing their lead
The report comes as Netanyahu's polling result worsens ahead of the election, with the latest Maariv poll showing the opposition bloc widening its lead to 54 seats while Netanyahu’s bloc dropped to 48.
The poll also found that 60% of respondents preferred a unity government if the October 27 election failed to produce a clear governing majority, while 23% preferred holding another election. Another 17% said they were undecided.
Of those who favored a unity government, 33% wanted a candidate from the opposition bloc to lead it, while 19% preferred Netanyahu to lead it. Another 8% favored a unity government regardless of who led it.
According to the polling results, Eisenkot led Netanyahu in a head-to-head matchup for prime minister, with 49% support compared with 41% for the incumbent.
Moshe Cohen contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Former deputy national security adviser discusses Netanyahu's reelection campaign
sources.text:
Former deputy national security adviser discusses Netanyahu's reelection campaign
NPR's Leila Fadel asks former Deputy National Security Adviser Jon Finer what a seventh term in office for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would mean for the U.S. and Israel.
LEILA FADEL, HOST:
Israel holds its national elections next week. It will be the country's first since the October 7 attacks by Hamas that triggered Israel's war in Gaza. Leading the country through it all has been Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He's fighting to stay in power for a seventh term, as many voters and political rivals accuse him of prolonging the war in Gaza and failing to prevent the attacks in the first place.
I sat down with the Biden administration's deputy national security adviser, Jon Finer, to ask him how he sees the future of the U.S.-Israel relationship and started by asking what it would mean if Netanyahu won again.
JON FINER: It would be a very good thing, I think, for Israel, for the United States and for the wider world if Prime Minister Netanyahu is defeated. His tenure has coincided with the October 7 attacks and the security breach that led to that, with the horrific conflict in Gaza that followed it and Israel's international standing growing only more and more isolated.
On the other hand, it is not clear that the cast of opposition leaders who are most likely to replace Netanyahu if he loses are going to make fundamental changes to Israeli policy that would improve the standing in the eyes of many Americans, who are turning rapidly against Israel. There are recent polls that show more than 60% of Americans now hold an unfavorable opinion of Israel. That number was 40% in 2022. And so it is not clear to me, even though it would be fundamentally a good thing for him to lose, that a new government would do enough to alter those trajectories.
FADEL: What would need to happen for there to be a fundamental shift that would change U.S. and global perception of Israel in this moment? I mean, like you said, more than 60% of U.S. voters, even in a recent survey, said they just want to stop military aid to Israel over what it's doing in Gaza and in its wars. When you say there need to be fundamental shifts, what are those?
FINER: So I can give you a few examples, all of which seem a bit like science fiction in the current moment. But, for example, there is not a single Jewish leader in Israel right now who endorses the idea of a Palestinian state. There is not a single leader who is likely to take on in a full-throated way the settlement enterprise in the West Bank. I think you would probably see a bit less settlement activity under an opposition-led government than you have seen under Netanyahu. But they are not likely to roll back what has been a just massive increase in the number of settlements in the West Bank, even just in the years since the October 7 attacks.
Similarly, when it comes to West Bank settler violence, I will give the opposition credit. They have said that it should stop. They have said that they will hold people accountable. But I was in the U.S. government working in the Biden administration the last time Netanyahu was out of office. And what we saw during that period, when we had a government called the change government led by some of the same leaders involved in the current opposition, was actually an increase in settlement activity from the Netanyahu government that had come before them and an increase in settler violence without a meaningful increase in accountability for that settler violence.
FADEL: I want to ask about one of your former colleagues - Brett McGurk, the former White House Middle East coordinator. He's - has a book out right now. And in that book, he blames Hamas pretty exclusively for the prolonged war and the inability to get a deal to free Israeli hostages. This is being used in this election cycle by Netanyahu's supporters to say, see. He did all he could after October 7 to get the hostages out, which was the main concern among Israelis. Do you agree with McGurk's assessment?
FINER: So look. I'm not going to get into a personal back-and-forth with Brett, who's somebody I worked with for a long time. But in my mind, both Hamas and the Netanyahu government were extremely reluctant to do a deal that would end the war and release the hostages. And there were definitely times, as apparently Brett described, according to your account of his book, where Hamas was the more reluctant party, said no to offers that were on the table that Israel may have accepted.
By the way, there were also clear times in which we believe that Hamas had basically agreed to the terms of a deal, and it was Israel and Prime Minister Netanyahu who added additional hurdles and additional aspects of the deal that made it impossible for that deal to occur. And the war went on for months longer than it needed to, and the hostages stayed in captivity. And some of them died during this extended period while the two sides continued to haggle.
FADEL: And thousands of Palestinians also died during that time.
FINER: Many thousands.
FADEL: There will be people listening to you right now, as we discuss the future of U.S.-Israeli relationship, who will say the Biden administration continued supplying Israel bombs and, for that reason, is responsible for the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians - men, women and children - as well as Israel's bombings of hospitals, of schools in Gaza, of entire buildings. How much blame does the administration that you served in bear for Israel's actions of the last few years?
FINER: I think everybody who served bears accountability for the - what happened during our time in office.
FADEL: Yeah.
FINER: And I'm, you know, not going to pretend otherwise. I do think, though, to say the least, U.S. policy towards Israel has not gotten better since our administration left office. Right now we have zero pressure placed by the Trump administration on Netanyahu to scale back what is essentially terrorism taking place by settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank. And obviously, we've had this collaboration on a deeply unpopular and unwise war with Iran. So this administration bears the responsibility for their choices that have led to these outcomes, as does every previous administration, including the one I served in.
FADEL: But did it create a permission structure that, basically, there won't be accountability?
FINER: I think the message that was sent is that the things that we were asking for - whether that is a different way to conduct the war in Gaza, whether that is increased humanitarian access to Gaza - were more akin to preferences than to interests. And future administrations should draw the lesson that absent concrete actions by the United States that make clear that lines have been crossed, left to its own devices, there are likely to be actions taken by Israel that violate American interests.
FADEL: Are there things you regret personally?
FINER: I mean, I regret some of the actions taken by the administration I served in. Administrations, at the end of the day, are decisions made by the very top. And I've made clear, I think, the ones that I think were misguided.
FADEL: There is a campaign right now basically calling for top administration officials from the Biden era to not be employed at think tanks and government positions, and I just wonder what you think about that.
FINER: Look, that is really a decision for other people to make. My view at this point is, when I'm asked to speak on this topic, I'm going to offer my opinion, my analysis based on the experiences that I've had, which have been quite a lot. You mentioned my time in the Biden administration. I also was John Kerry's chief of staff.
FADEL: Yeah.
FINER: The last time we had real negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians - spoiler alert - ultimately unsuccessful, as every other negotiation before that had been. And so I'm less focused on what this means in terms of this or that future political role and more focused on trying to make the case for what I believe would be the right policy approach. And people have the right to listen to that or not.
FADEL: Jon Finer, thank you for your time.
FINER: Thank you.
(SOUNDBITE OF ACETONE'S "MIDNIGHT COWBOY")
FADEL: Jon Finer was the deputy national security adviser in the Biden administration.
(SOUNDBITE OF ACETONE'S "MIDNIGHT COWBOY")
